welcome.title: Welcome
welcome.body: This app turns an area of OpenStreetMap into printable territory cards. The short version: find a place, download its streets and buildings, split it into territories, print one card each. A few short steps follow — Esc leaves at any point.

toolbar.title: One panel for the tools
toolbar.body: Everything the app does is in here, grouped by what it is for: the area, the territories, what is shown, undo and redo, files, the app itself. A tool you cannot use yet is greyed out rather than hidden, and its tooltip says what is missing. The arrow at the top folds the panel away when the map needs the room.

search.title: Start with a search
search.body: Type a town, a district or a street. When OpenStreetMap has an official outline for the place, the app offers it as your outer boundary — faster and more accurate than tracing one by hand.

draw.title: Or draw the boundary
draw.body: Click to place corners — Backspace takes the last one back and Esc abandons the shape — then Enter or a double-click closes it. Everything else the app does happens inside this outer boundary. It is not final: click this button again — or right-click the boundary — to move, add or delete its corners.

locate.title: Find yourself
locate.body: Centres the map on your current position — handy when you are starting in the neighborhood you are standing in.

refetch.title: Download the map data
refetch.body: Fetches the streets and building footprints inside the boundary from OpenStreetMap. You are asked once automatically after drawing; this button repeats it after you change the boundary.

sample.title: A sample to work on
sample.body: The next few screens only exist once there is an area loaded, so the app has borrowed a made-up village for a minute — the streets are called "Sample street" for a reason. Nothing of yours has been touched: whatever was on the map is put back at the end, and none of this is saved.

partitionButton.title: The Split button
partitionButton.body: Territories start here. The button wakes up once there is a boundary with data inside it — until then it is grey and says why. Pressing it opens the dialog on the next step.

partition.title: Split into territories
partition.body: This is the real dialog, opened on the sample by the button still outlined behind it. It divides the area automatically — either into territories of roughly N buildings each, or into a fixed number of roughly equal size. The cuts follow real streets rather than straight lines.

cutButton.title: The Cut button
cutButton.body: Turns on the cut tool for correcting a split by hand, and stays lit for as long as the tool is on — pressing it again is one of the ways back out. It needs at least one territory to work on.

cut.title: Correct a split by hand
cut.body: The button is lit and the tool is on: this bar at the bottom of the map is the tool. You draw a line across a territory and it divides; the line snaps to junctions, streets and existing edges, S, B and F switch the three kinds of snapping, Alt places a free point, Backspace takes the last one back, and Enter makes the cut.

mergeButton.title: The Merge button
mergeButton.body: The other direction: two territories that should have been one. It needs at least two to choose between, and like Cut it stays lit for as long as the mode is running.

merge.title: Join territories
merge.body: Merge mode is on and the button is lit. Click two or more neighboring territories and this bar merges them into one, dissolving the edges they shared.

territory.title: Every territory has a menu
territory.body: This is what a right-click on a territory gives you: zoom to it, print it, mark it as done, or delete it. Hovering over a street or a building instead shows what OpenStreetMap knows about it — the name, the address, the surface.

printMenu.title: Printing starts here
printMenu.body: There is no print button in the toolbar, because a card is always the card of one particular territory — so printing starts in that territory's own menu. This entry opens the card view for the one you right-clicked.

print.title: The card
print.body: The preview can be panned, zoomed and rotated; the settings beside it set the label size and the border, erase stretches that run through a house, and take the locality and territory number. That number stays with the territory: the next card offers it back, and the wall map writes it. Load your own PDF form and the map is placed into it. A territory whose card has been made turns green and carries a tick.

clearPrinted.title: The next round
clearPrinted.body: The green fill and the tick are marks, not geometry, so doing an area again is the same territories with the marks cleared. This button clears them all at once; a single territory is unmarked from its own menu. It asks first, and Ctrl+Z will not bring the marks back.

restore.title: And back to your own map
restore.body: The sample is gone and your own work is back exactly as it was. Leaving the tour early does the same thing, so there is never a wrong moment to press Escape.

history.title: Undo anything
history.body: Undo and redo step back through boundary edits, cuts and merges, and Ctrl+Z works too. Inside the cut tool, the outline editor and the eraser they take back points, corners and strokes instead, so undo always means whatever you last did.

notesButton.title: Notes on the map
notesButton.body: Not everything worth knowing about a round is a boundary. A gate round the back, a block with no letterbox, the side of a street somebody else is walking — this is where those go. Notes lie over the territories rather than inside them, so splitting, cutting and merging leave every one of them exactly where it was put. This sample carries three.

notes.title: Four pens
notes.body: A note is a sentence pinned to a spot, a pin marks one place or building, the pencil draws along the ground, and the last pen writes a caption straight onto the map. Drag the pencil for a freehand line or click point by point; with “Snap to streets” on, each clicked point jumps onto the road network and the line follows the road between them, so a mark lies on the street rather than near it. “Freeform” goes the other way: only the hand draws, and a click places nothing. A finished mark wears the same handles the boundary does — drag a point to move it, click one to take it out, and drag the dot halfway along a straight hop to bend it. While the pencil has the left button, the right one pans the map. Everything here is saved with the project and comes out on the card: drawn onto a PNG, and on a PDF as real comments a reader can open, move or delete.

layers.title: What is shown
layers.body: This group is the picture rather than the work. The pair at the top steps the map in and out, and the drop-down beside them chooses what is under it — the map itself, aerial imagery, terrain — since only one thing can be under it at a time. The aid layers are for the screen only: a card is always printed on the OpenStreetMap layer. Below the line, each switch takes one thing off the map without taking it out of the project: the boundary, the streets, the houses, the territory shapes.

info.title: Where you stand
info.body: How many streets, buildings and territories are loaded, with a hint about the sensible next step. The warning mark beside the territory count means something needs a second look — here it is the patch of ground no territory covers. That count is a button, and it is the shortest way to the territory list, where every such fault is named, found and repaired. The panel is hidden on a window too narrow for it; the Print button in the toolbar opens the same list.

files.title: Take your work with you
files.body: Export writes the boundary, the downloaded data and every territory to one GeoJSON file. That is how work gets backed up, and the first half of how it moves between devices.

importFiles.title: … and bring it back
importFiles.body: Import reads such a file back in - or a printed card, which carries the project inside it. With something already on the map it asks whether to add to it or replace it, and several files can be picked at once: that is how the villages of a circuit end up in one project. Reshaping, trimming and splitting then work on one of them at a time - the one you are looking at.

reset.title: Start over
reset.body: Clears the boundary, the downloaded data and every territory. It asks first, and it cannot be undone.

language.title: Multiple languages
language.body: English, Polish, German and French. The choice is part of the address, so a link you share opens in the language you were using.

offline.title: Works offline
offline.body: The app can be installed like a native one and keeps working without a connection: your boundary, data and territories survive a reload, and map tiles you have already seen stay cached. Downloading new data and building PDFs still need the network.

done.title: That is everything
done.body: This button reopens the tour whenever you want it. Leave the box below ticked and it will not open by itself again.

trimButton.title: Trim the boundary
trimButton.body: A boundary you draw or adopt always covers more than you meant: fields, forest, the farms across the river. Splitting all of it wastes territories on empty ground. This button reshapes the boundary around the buildings first.

trim.title: Ignore what you do not need
trim.body: Click buildings to exclude them, or shift-drag a box over a whole edge of the map. Each one gets a mark you can click to put it back, whatever the zoom. Green is what you keep, red is what you give up.

trimSliders.title: What the sliders set
trimSliders.body: Two sliders shape the new boundary — how far behind the houses it runs, and how much its edge is straightened — and two more set what the automatic pass excludes for you: how far out a building has to stand to count as isolated, and the largest group it may drop in one go. With "Follow streets" on, the boundary snaps onto the road network instead of cutting through gardens.

trimMarks.title: The marks show what is being dropped
trimMarks.body: The isolated farms out along the track were excluded automatically, and each one carries a mark that stays the same size however far you zoom out. Click a mark to keep that building after all — the boundary reshapes around it, along the track, rather than pretending it is not there.

trimEdit.title: Or move the corners yourself
trimEdit.body: No slider can express the one corner that should follow the ditch rather than the hedge, so this box — or E — hands you the proposed boundary itself. Every corner of it grows a handle: drag one to move it, click one to delete it, drag the small dot on an edge to add one. Those same three gestures reshape the boundary itself a few steps from here. The sliders lock while you hold the shape, because recomputing it would throw your adjustment away; clearing the box goes back to the computed outline.

outlineButton.title: Or reshape the one you have
outlineButton.body: The same button reopens the boundary once one exists. It is the answer to a corner in the wrong place, and it is the reason a boundary traced from an administrative outline is a starting point rather than something you are stuck with.

outline.title: Move the corners
outline.body: Every corner of the boundary now carries a handle, and with a mouse the pointer says what each one does: an open hand over a corner, a plus over the small dot halfway along an edge. Drag a corner and it moves — the outline, the corner count and the change in area follow the drag. Click a corner and it is gone; the last three stay, because two corners are a line rather than an area. Drag one of those dots and the edge bends around the corner it leaves behind.

outlineErase.title: Rub out a whole run
outlineErase.body: A boundary adopted from an official outline can carry hundreds of corners, and straightening one stretch of it is twenty clicks, each of which moves the remaining handles under your hand. So hold X and sweep instead: a red ring follows the pointer, every corner it touches goes, and the whole sweep is a single undo. The bar keeps the rest — the corner count and how far the area has moved, an undo and a redo for one corner change at a time, Reset for the shape you started with, and Apply. Applying clips the territories to the new outline; growing past what was downloaded offers to fetch the rest.

numbers.title: Number them
numbers.body: Puts each territory's number on the map, so counting them is reading rather than searching. A number chip is a second handle on its territory: it hovers, selects and opens the same menu as the shape underneath, and it carries the tick once a card has been made.

gaps.title: Ground nobody covers
gaps.body: Deleting a territory, cutting one thin or growing the boundary all leave patches that belong to no card, and nothing about them looks wrong on screen — you find out when a street is on no card at all. This switch draws them in dashed orange, and there is one in this sample, out in the field east of the village. Clicking a patch turns it into a territory, and they are rows in the territory list as well.

shortcuts.title: What can I press?
shortcuts.body: This tour explains the workflow once; that button answers the other question, every time. The list is grouped by tool with the one you are in at the top, and it is generated from the same registry that runs the keys — so it cannot drift out of date. ? or F1 opens it from anywhere.

printButton.title: Printing a card
printButton.body: This opens the territory list with a printer beside every row, which is the way in when you know which number you want. The same view is one right-click away on the territory itself.

territoryList.title: The territory list
territoryList.body: Two ways in: the Print button in the toolbar, or the territory count in the panel at the bottom right. One row per territory, in the order the numbers run. A row walks the map to its territory, the printer beside it makes the card, and the flags say what is wrong with it — drawn in separate pieces, no buildings in it, too small to label, or ground that is in no territory at all. The chips above filter to exactly those rows, so ninety-nine territories become the four worth a second look.

autoheal.title: Repairing the whole list
autoheal.body: Three faults are mechanical enough to repair without asking, and this button does all of them at once: a territory drawn in separate pieces becomes one territory per piece, a territory with no buildings is absorbed into the neighbor it shares the most boundary with, and a patch that belongs to nobody is adopted first and then judged by those same two rules — which is how the empty field east of the village ends up part of the territory beside it.

autohealScope.title: One undo, or one row
autohealScope.body: The whole repair is a single undo, and the wand on one row does the same for that row alone. To get back to this list at any time: the Print button in the toolbar, or the territory count in the panel at the bottom right.

wallCard.title: One sheet for the wall
wallCard.body: Draws every territory of the project onto a single sheet, up to A0. The same preview as a card - pan, zoom, rotate, scale bar, compass - with the sheet size chosen beside it. Each territory is marked with whatever its card called it, or with its number until a card has been made. Nothing is marked as printed, so the record of which cards have been handed out survives.

about.title: About OSM Territory Mapper
about.purpose: Splits a map area into walkable territories and prints each one as a PDF card. Boundaries follow real streets, so a territory is something a person can be asked to walk. Streets and buildings come from OpenStreetMap.
